description: Press forming, sand casting, die casting and injection moulding — stages and where each fits.
content_html:
Four Distinct Families

Shaping, casting and moulding all give material a new form without removing it as waste chips — but the mechanisms are completely different. A common exam error is mixing stages from different processes. Keep these four families separate from the start:

  • Press forming — squeeze a sheet between two solid dies to change its shape in the solid state.
  • Injection moulding — melt polymer granules and inject under pressure into a closed metal mould.
  • Sand casting — pour liquid metal into a cavity formed by compressing sand around a pattern.
  • Pressure die casting — inject liquid metal under high pressure into a precision reusable steel die.

Press Forming (and Related Sheet-Metal Operations)

Press forming places a flat sheet of metal between a punch (upper male tool) and a die (lower female tool). The press ram drives the punch down with enormous force — hundreds of tonnes for structural pressings — deforming the sheet permanently into the die cavity. The car body panel on every modern car is made this way: the outer skin of a vehicle door takes less than a second to press from a flat steel blank. Related sheet-metal operations include:

  • Bending and folding — a press-brake bends sheet along a straight line; a box-and-pan folder creates enclosure cases and duct sections.
  • Punching and blanking — a punch shears a hole (punching) or cuts a shaped blank (blanking) from sheet stock in a single stroke.
  • Stamping — a high-speed press stamps (embosses or cuts) repeated features — such as the tabs on a battery connector — into sheet at production rates of thousands per hour.
  • Composite lay-up — individual layers of glass-fibre or carbon-fibre cloth pre-impregnated with resin (“prepreg”) are laid by hand into a mould, then cured under heat and pressure in an autoclave. Used for F1 monocoques and wind-turbine blades where weight is critical.
Key Fact

Press forming acts on solid sheet metal between a punch and die. Vacuum forming stretches a heated thermoplastic sheet over a single mould using atmospheric pressure. Injection moulding melts polymer and injects it under pressure into a closed mould. These are three distinct processes — mixing their stages in an answer loses marks.

Sand Casting

Sand casting is one of the oldest manufacturing processes still used today. A replica of the desired part — the pattern — is placed inside a two-part wooden or metal moulding box (the cope and drag). Sand mixed with a bonding agent is rammed tightly around the pattern. The pattern is then removed, leaving a cavity. If the part requires an internal void (such as a pipe bore), a separate core of sand is placed inside the cavity. The two halves are clamped together.

Molten metal is poured in through the sprue (the vertical channel), flows along the runner (horizontal channel) and enters the mould cavity through the gate. A riser (also called a feeder) is an additional reservoir of molten metal that compensates for shrinkage as the casting cools. Once solidified and cooled, the sand is broken away and the casting is removed. A draft angle on the pattern walls is essential to release the pattern cleanly from the sand without crumbling the cavity walls. The casting is then fettled (excess metal from sprues and runners is cut away) and may be machined to final dimensions.

  1. Place the pattern in the drag (lower half of moulding box) and ram sand tightly around it.
  2. Fit the cope (upper half) and form the sprue and riser channels using pegs.
  3. Remove the pattern carefully, leaving the cavity. Place any sand cores required for internal features.
  4. Reassemble cope and drag; secure together.
  5. Pour molten metal (e.g. cast iron, aluminium alloy) through the sprue until metal appears at the riser.
  6. Allow to cool and solidify fully.
  7. Break away the sand mould; retrieve the casting. Cut off sprues, runners and risers. Fettle and finish.

Pressure Die Casting

Pressure die casting injects molten metal — typically aluminium, zinc or magnesium alloy — under high pressure (10–200 MPa) into a hardened steel die. The die is precision-machined and can be reused for tens of thousands of cycles. The high pressure forces metal into fine detail and thin sections that gravity alone cannot fill. The cooling rate is much faster than sand casting (the steel die conducts heat quickly), giving a finer grain structure and better mechanical properties.

Advantages over sand casting: better surface finish, tighter dimensional tolerance, faster cycle time (seconds per part vs minutes), reusable die. Limitations: the steel die costs tens of thousands of pounds to make, so die casting is only economical at high volumes. It is also limited to non-ferrous metals — the high melting point of steel would destroy a steel die. Gearbox housings, engine covers and tap bodies are typical die-cast products.

Injection Moulding

Injection moulding is the dominant process for producing plastic parts at high volume. Polymer granules are fed from a hopper into a heated barrel where a reciprocating screw melts and homogenises them. When sufficient melt has accumulated, the screw acts as a plunger, injecting the melt under high pressure through the gate into the closed mould cavity. The mould is water-cooled, so the part solidifies in seconds. The mould then opens and ejector pins push the part free. Cycle times are typically 15–60 seconds for most consumer products.

Critical design features for injection moulding: the mould must have a draft angle on all walls so the part releases cleanly; wall thickness should be uniform to avoid sink marks and warping; internal ribs increase stiffness without adding bulk. The mould tool costs £20,000–£200,000 but is amortised across millions of parts. This process produces everything from mobile phone cases to car dashboards.

Key Fact

Injection moulding and pressure die casting both use a reusable precision metal die/mould; sand casting uses a single-use sand mould that is destroyed each cycle. The reusable die gives better surface finish and tighter tolerances but requires high capital investment.

Press forming: solid sheet metal, punch-and-die, high volume, excellent for thin-wall structural shapes.

Sand casting: any metal incl. ferrous, low tooling cost, disposable mould, low-to-medium volume, rough surface finish requiring machining.

Pressure die casting: non-ferrous metals only, reusable steel die, high volume, fine detail, fast cycle, high tooling cost.

Injection moulding: thermoplastics, reusable steel mould, very high volume, fine detail, fast cycle, high tooling cost, draft angles essential.
exam_tip_html: The biggest mistake in shaping/moulding questions is mixing up process stages. For press forming: punch-and-die, solid sheet, high force. For injection moulding: melt-and-inject polymer into a closed mould. For sand casting: pattern, sand mould, pour liquid metal, break mould. For pressure die casting: inject liquid metal into reusable steel die under high pressure. If an exam question describes “vacuum forming” stages alongside injection moulding, recognise these are wrong — draw a mental line between the four families before writing your answer. Always include the draft angle as a key design feature for any process involving a mould or die.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Press forming squeezes solid sheet metal between a punch and die. Injection moulding melts polymer and injects it into a closed metal mould. Sand casting pours liquid metal into a disposable sand mould. Pressure die casting injects liquid metal into a reusable precision steel die — keep these stages separate.
  • The draft angle is essential on mould patterns and die walls so the solidified part or pattern releases cleanly without damaging the mould cavity.
  • Sand casting suits ferrous metals and low volumes (cheap tooling); pressure die casting and injection moulding suit high volumes (expensive reusable tooling amortised across many parts).

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes pressure die casting?
A) Molten metal is poured by gravity into a disposable sand mould
B) Molten metal is injected under high pressure into a precision reusable steel die
C) Sheet metal is squeezed between a punch and die in the solid state
D) Polymer granules are melted and injected into a water-cooled mould
practice_questions.marks: B) Molten metal is injected under high pressure into a precision reusable steel die [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the channel through which molten metal is poured into a sand mould, and name the reservoir that compensates for metal shrinkage during cooling.
practice_questions.marks:
Sprue (vertical pouring channel) [1 mark].
Riser / feeder (reservoir that compensates for shrinkage) [1 mark].
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the stages of producing an aluminium component using sand casting.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award one mark each for any four stages in a logical order:
- Place the pattern in the drag; ram sand around it
- Add cope, form sprue and riser channels; separate halves and remove pattern
- Place any cores required for internal voids; reassemble and secure mould
- Pour molten aluminium through the sprue until metal rises at the riser
- Allow to cool and solidify; break away the sand mould
- Remove casting; cut off sprues and risers; fettle and machine to final dimensions
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a draft angle is needed on the pattern used in sand casting and on the walls of an injection mould.
practice_questions.marks:
Sand casting: a draft angle on the pattern walls allows the pattern to be withdrawn cleanly from the compacted sand without collapsing the cavity walls [1 mark].
Injection moulding: a draft angle on the mould wall allows the solidified plastic part to be ejected (pushed out by ejector pins) without jamming or tearing [1 mark].
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Vantage Enclosures Ltd manufactures aluminium housings for outdoor electrical distribution boxes. The current production volume is 200 units per year, but a new contract would increase this to 15,000 units per year. The company currently uses sand casting.

Evaluate whether the company should switch to pressure die casting for the higher volume. In your answer, consider tooling cost, surface finish, dimensional accuracy, production rate and any limitations.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced evaluation of both processes with clear links to the scenario details (200 vs 15,000 units/year; aluminium; outdoor electrical housing). Both advantages and limitations addressed for each process. A justified conclusion with reasoning about when the switch becomes economical.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both processes described with some comparison. Most key factors covered. Conclusion present but reasoning may be limited.

Developing (3-4 marks): Mostly descriptive. One process favoured without clear comparison. Scenario details used minimally.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Generic points about casting with little or no link to the scenario.

Content that may be credited:
Sand casting: low tooling cost (just the pattern), suitable for low volumes, but slower per part, rough surface finish, less dimensional accuracy, mould destroyed each cycle.
Pressure die casting: high tooling cost (steel die, tens of thousands of pounds), but at 15,000 units/year the cost per part is much lower; faster cycle time (seconds); better surface finish and tighter tolerances suitable for precision enclosures; die lasts tens of thousands of cycles.
Limitation of die casting: suitable for aluminium (non-ferrous) so material is compatible; but design changes require expensive die modification.
Conclusion: at 200 units/year sand casting is appropriate; at 15,000 units/year the die cost is easily amortised and die casting is the better choice for speed, accuracy and consistency.

practice_questions.text: Compare injection moulding and press forming as processes for manufacturing a 1 mm thick flat cover panel. In your answer, consider the material used, the tooling required, the production rate and the type of industries that use each process.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Compare Two Processes or Methods
practice_questions.marks:
Material: injection moulding uses thermoplastics (e.g. ABS, polypropylene); press forming uses sheet metal (steel, aluminium).
Tooling: both require an expensive metal tool (injection mould; punch and die set) suitable for high-volume production.
Production rate: both are fast once tooling is set up — injection moulding cycles in 15-60 seconds; press forming can stamp thousands of panels per hour on high-speed presses.
Industries: injection moulding dominates consumer electronics, packaging and automotive interior trim; press forming dominates automotive body panels, white-goods casings and structural metalwork.
Key difference: injection moulding cannot produce metal panels; press forming cannot produce polymer parts. Material dictates the process.
[6 marks — 1 mark per valid point; 2 marks for a developed comparative point. Marks awarded for comparison, not description in isolation.]

knowledge_checks.q: Which process uses a punch and die to shape solid sheet metal?
Why is sand casting unsuitable for producing the same part as pressure die casting at high volumes?
options: Sand casting cannot use aluminium alloys
The sand mould is destroyed each cycle, making it slow and labour-intensive at high volume
Sand casting produces parts that are too large
Sand casting requires a very expensive steel die

knowledge_checks.q: In sand casting, the replica of the finished part placed into the sand to form the cavity is called the _____.
In injection moulding, a _____ on the mould walls allows the solidified part to be ejected without jamming.
Match each process to its key characteristic:
right: Disposable sand mould; suitable for ferrous and non-ferrous metals
Reusable steel die; non-ferrous metals injected under high pressure
Polymer granules melted and injected into a water-cooled metal mould

flashcard_questions.a: Forcing solid sheet metal between a punch and die under high press force to produce a 3D shape.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the pattern in sand casting?
flashcard_questions.a: A replica of the finished part used to form the cavity in the sand mould.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the sprue in sand casting?
flashcard_questions.a: The vertical channel through which molten metal is poured into the mould.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of the riser (feeder) in sand casting?
flashcard_questions.a: A reservoir of molten metal that compensates for shrinkage as the casting cools.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a draft angle essential on sand casting patterns?
flashcard_questions.a: It allows the pattern to be withdrawn from the sand without collapsing the cavity walls.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is pressure die casting limited to non-ferrous metals?
flashcard_questions.a: The high melting point of ferrous metals would destroy the steel die.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the typical cycle time for injection moulding a consumer product?
What does the screw do in an injection moulding machine?
flashcard_questions.a: It melts the polymer granules and acts as a plunger to inject the melt into the mould.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one advantage of pressure die casting over sand casting.
flashcard_questions.a: Better surface finish, tighter tolerances and faster cycle time per part.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of material is used in composite lay-up?
flashcard_questions.a: Layers of carbon-fibre or glass-fibre cloth pre-impregnated with resin (prepreg).

flashcard_questions.q: What does punching produce in sheet metal, and what does blanking produce?
flashcard_questions.a: Punching makes a hole; blanking cuts out a shaped blank from the sheet.

glossary_terms.definition: A manufacturing process in which sheet metal is forced between a punch and a die under high press force to produce a 3D shape in the solid state.
A replica of the finished part, slightly oversized to allow for metal shrinkage, used to form the cavity in a sand mould.
A tapered angle on the side walls of a mould pattern that allows it to be withdrawn from the sand without collapsing the mould cavity.
A casting process in which molten metal is injected under high pressure into a precision steel die that is reused many thousands of times.
